subject: dragonBoat
pitch:
Category: Vehicle.
Subject: dragon boat with drummer and paddles.
Style: Chinese festival lacquer.
reasoning:
I'm sketching out a TypeScript module for a dragon boat scene with a drummer and paddlers in Chinese festival lacquer style, planning proportions like a roughly 10m long, 1.1m wide hull to keep the model thorough yet manageable.

Since this is a vehicle/prop rather than a creature, I decide to keep it as a static model without joints for safety and simplicity. I'm orienting the boat along the +Z axis with the hull resting at the waterline, and thinking through how to loft the hull cross-sections with a canoe-like shape rising from the keel to the sides, bow and stern curving upward.

For the actual hull construction, I settle on a solid elliptical loft in lacquered red for the main shell, with gold and black sweeps along the sides forming gunwale rails, plus a darker inset floor strip and thwarts for the paddlers to sit on. I'm working through the geometry math to figure out where the interior floor plane should sit relative to the elliptical hull curve so it reads as an open boat rather than a solid blob.

I could instead slice the hull into frustumBox segments to capture the upswept bow, or try a sweep with a box-shaped section whose half-extents vary along a catmull path tracing the keel's curve upward at the bow.

With the box section, the path's binormal/normal frame naturally gives flat sides and a flat top/bottom, which works well even as the frame rotates near the bow. I'll build the hull as such a sweep from stern to bow, then add gunwale rails on top to give it that hollow-boat look.

I'm planning the hull finish with red lacquer paint, a gold stripe near the sheer line, and repeating cloud/scroll decals along the sides to evoke traditional dragon boat decoration. Then I'm working out the keel curve, setting the centerline height and hull thickness so the bottom sits flush at midship while rising toward the bow and stern.

I need to make sure the lowest point stays just above the floor, keeping the exact middle flat at zero while tapering the width and depth toward the ends—so as the radius shrinks, the center height has to adjust to keep the bottom aligned correctly along the path.

Defining the width profile along the hull...

I'm working out the prow geometry so the bow rises upward appropriately, adjusting the curvature factor to keep the upturned front from looking too extreme, then planning a dragon head mounted on top of the raised neck at the bow.

Now I'm sketching the dragon head details: a neck sweep rising from the prow to the skull position, painted red lacquer with gold scale patterns and a gold collar ring, plus a tail curl at the stern built with a similar sweep technique.

I'm planning the nose details with upturned nostril bumps, then building separate upper and lower jaws with cone-shaped teeth rows and a tongue, plus bulging eyes with dark pupils and brow ridges positioned on the skull.

For antlers, I'm branching gold-cream sweeps from the skull top with tined ends and red tips. For the mane, I'm placing flame-like spike blades along the neck using an extruded profile swept along a path, oriented backward and upward.

For coloring, I'm painting a gradient across the flame outline, blending orange at the base to gold at the tips. I'm adding a beard of tapering white bezier tufts hanging under the chin, plus two golden curving whisker sweeps drooping back from each side of the snout, and considering a flaming pearl placed in front of the creature.

I'll skip the pearl and forehead tassel, opting instead for a small gold forehead emblem built from shapes rather than CJK text since font rendering support might be unreliable, and I'm painting an auspicious swirl motif on the drum using paths. For the tail, I'm sweeping a curling catmull-rom curve upward from the stern.

Now I'm planning a fish-like tail with scale painting, fin blades along the back, and a flame-tipped end made of three blade shapes, then moving on to boat body details like gunwale rails built from hull sweeps, working out the clock-angle convention for positioning the box-section sides relative to the tube's orientation.

Still writing hull geometry functions...

Still writing hull paint logic...

Working out the viewer orientation math, I confirm that with the viewer facing -X, the bow (+Z) ends up on their left side — minor detail for symmetric cloud placement. Now I'm sketching the gold swirling ruyi cloud motifs for the decal.

Adjusting the stroke curve and now thinking through the hull's interior floor—a dark lacquer box between the gunwales that needs to follow the same sweep path as the hull top but slightly narrower and raised, so it reads correctly at the rising ends rather than just sitting flat.

Adding dashed gold trim striping...

Now I'm thinking through the paddler count for the dragon boat crew — roughly 20 paddlers plus drummer, steerer, and flag bearer.

Benches sit as thin red lacquered slabs with gold trim at the rail tops, around y=0.6, slightly above the floor level. I'm working out paddler posture: hip at bench height, torso leaning forward with head up around 1.25, and legs bent with thighs reaching forward and shins dropping to meet the floor near y=0.5.

I'm running into a geometry problem though -- the gap between bench and floor is only about 9cm, too shallow for a realistic seated pose, since the hull isn't deep enough there. Raising the bench or deepening the floor well would require either taller hull walls or carving an interior cavity, so I need to rethink the hull proportions to make room for a believable seated posture.

Instead of a solid lofted hull, I'm switching to building it from actual wall and floor pieces: a bottom sweep forming the floor, two side sweeps forming the walls, with solid blocks capping the bow and stern to close off the ends. The outer walls get lacquer red, the floor interior stays dark, and I'm placing the paddler benches spanning wall-to-wall at a height that sits realistically above the floor inside the hollowed-out hull.

For the hull bottom slab, I'll paint the top face dark (floor color) where the normal points up, and use the red scheme elsewhere. At the bow, I want the walls to converge down to zero width.

The wall thickness is 0.03 so with walls on each side, they nearly touch in the middle, giving a narrow solid prow look. I'll leave the dragon neck sweep to handle the bow's stem post rather than adding a separate block.

Now I'm planning the gunwale cap along the wall tops with a wider lip and black/gold striping, plus outer decals aligned to the wall's outer face. For wall coloring, I'll paint based on height from the waterline—gold above, black near the rim, and a dark band at the base—while possibly darkening inner faces using the normal direction.

For the hull sections, I'm working out how the wall path's z-parameter relates to arc length along the rising bow and stern, deciding it's close enough to approximate linearly despite small discrepancies. Since wall height stays constant regardless of position, I realize the radius function doesn't need to depend on t for the walls, though the floor slab's width still varies along z, so I need a separate function for that.

I'm defining a rise function for the stern and bow curvature, computing that the prow top reaches about 1.14 with the neck beginning near z=5.1, and now I'm moving on to placing the benches along the hull.

Next I'm placing bench rows at the specified z positions and situating a drummer platform near the bow around z=3.9, calculating the hull radius there to make sure the drum stand fits within the narrowing walls.

Checking the paddlers face forward toward the dragon head, so nothing blocks their view, while the drummer faces backward. For the paddlers' faces, I'll keep it simple with small dark eye dots on sphere heads, plus headbands and colored team shirts for visual distinction.

Since there's no water plane defined, the paddle blades can't dip below y=0 given the sink constraint, so I'll pose everyone mid-stroke with paddles raised in a synchronized forward-angled position rather than dipping into water.

Now I'm working out seated paddler geometry facing forward, starting with the hip/pelvis block at the seat position.

For the torso, I'm leaning it forward from the hips with widening shoulders, and thinking through team jersey colors—aiming for a festive palette with bright reds, golds, and jade tones to match the boat's lacquer-red hue.

Now I'm figuring out the head and neck: a skin-toned sphere for the head, a hemisphere cap for black hair, and a thin red torus band around the forehead as a headband. I'm also sketching how shoulders connect to arms, working out the paddler's hand placement on the shaft and T-grip depending on which side they're paddling.

I'm working out the blade geometry as a flat frustum box attached past the shaft end, trying to figure out the correct orientation so the blade's wide face is perpendicular to the paddle's stroke direction rather than edge-on.

Defining the paddle blade outline with a widening leaf shape and sharp tip, avoiding automatic smoothing to prevent self-intersection errors.

I'm now thinking about coloring the blade using the extrusion's local coordinates, giving it a red body with a gold tip band, and tallying up the body parts needed per paddler—pelvis, torso, head, hair, headband, eyes, shoulders, arms, hands, legs, feet, plus the paddle shaft and blade.

That brings me to roughly 600 total parts across all paddlers, which should stay safely under the limit, though I want to trim where possible—skipping separate shoulder spheres and instead sweeping each arm as a single bent capsule through the shoulder, elbow, and hand points, since without joints a sweep just bends smoothly at the corners. I'll do the same for legs, sweeping a polyline through hip, knee, and ankle with a slightly thicker radius.

Totaling parts per paddler: pelvis, torso, head, hair, band, two eyes, two arms, two legs, two feet, paddle shaft, and blade comes to fifteen, so sixteen paddlers gives 240 parts, which is manageable if I keep sweep sides low (six instead of the default) to control triangle count. I'm now working out shoulder and hand placement geometry—figuring out inner versus outer shoulder x-coordinates relative to torso width and hull position so the arms reach naturally to the paddle on the outboard side.

I'm narrowing the torso to 0.30 wide with shoulders at ±0.14 offset, widening the hull's mid radius to 0.55 for a roughly 10:1 length-to-width ratio matching a real canoe, and now working through where the upper and lower grip hands sit relative to the shoulders and paddle line to get a believable forward-leaning paddling pose.

Checking the outer shoulder position and verifying the upper hand reach from the inner shoulder to the grip point gives a plausible arm length around 0.55.

I'm also checking the elbow bend geometry and confirming the paddle clears the wall at x=±0.55 with enough margin, while the shaft and blade dimensions stay consistent across the row-spaced paddles.

Blade geometry runs from 0.9 to 1.24 along its length, giving a tip height of 1.24, so I'm adding a small perpendicular T-grip rod at the handle base, sized about 0.12 across with a wood color, then planning simple black hair caps for the paddlers.

For the hair, I'll use a slightly larger partial sphere positioned a bit back and up from the head center, scaled down vertically so it covers the top and back while leaving the front face exposed.

For headwear, I'm considering an open cylindrical ring to act as a headband, positioned around the forehead area with outward-facing normals so it's visible as a thin band.

For the face, I'm placing small dark eye spheres at calculated positions based on the head sphere's curvature, embedding them just under the surface. I'm also thinking about adding a stripe or trim detail down the shirt's front for visual interest.

Now I'm designing the drummer: seated on the bow platform facing inward, dressed in black and gold with a headband, holding two sticks to strike a large barrel drum mounted on a stand.

The hull gets too narrow near the bow for the drummer to fit comfortably, so I'm trying repositioning both drum and drummer further back where the hull width and floor rise are more forgiving, checking that the drum's radius still clears the walls at its new location.

The stern mirrors the same curve profile, with the tail ending symmetrically at -5.2. For the drummer's seat, I'm placing a raised stool platform at z=4.15, computing the floor height there and setting the stool top accordingly, with the drum positioned above on a red A-frame stand.

Now I'm positioning the drummer's torso, head, and arms holding sticks, working out hand positions relative to the drum head's surface and angling the sticks downward toward it, with one stick raised up for a sense of motion.

I'm designing the drum itself as a lathed barrel shape with a red lacquer body, rows of gold rivets, and cream skin heads featuring a painted triple-swirl pattern visible from both ends, defining the lathe outline coordinates for the body's profile.

Adding gold trim rings and studs...

For the drum heads I'm placing textured circles facing outward at the barrel ends, designing a tomoe-style swirl pattern with three comma shapes rotated around the center using arc paths.

Simplifying to a yin-yang design with gold and red curves, dots, and an outer ring stroke seems cleaner. I'm also checking the overall model proportions, making sure the dragon head and antlers don't push the bounding box too large.

Now I'm placing the helmsman at the stern, standing on the slightly raised platform there, holding a long steering oar that extends down toward the water behind the boat. I want to make sure his head height and the oar's position stay within reasonable bounds, and I'm dressing him in a traditional dark jacket to fit the dragon boat theme.

I'm also considering adding a pennant flag near the stern, waving with a slight curve to suggest motion, using a simple painted emblem instead of any text to avoid rendering issues with characters.

Adding a small hanging tassel under the dragon's chin, plus a pair of glowing lanterns on the stern poles. For textures I'm sketching out a small set: gold cloud decals, dragon eye, drum swirl, a forehead emblem, pennant emblem, and a beard/tuft card, keeping the count around 5-12.

I'm also considering a waterline band done through procedural painting rather than a decal—using a sine function along the hull's z-position to create scalloped cream-colored wave shapes near the bottom of the hull instead of a separate wave texture.

Now I'm counting up the total textures needed (loud markings, eye, drum, forehead pearl, flag emblem, mane tuft) and deciding six is probably enough, maybe adding a scale pattern via paint for the neck rather than another texture. Then I start defining the color palette for the lacquer paint, working out red, deep red, and gold hex values along with how the paint should blend gloss highlights based on surface normal and slight noise.

I'm fleshing out the full palette with gold, black, cream, jade, teal, skin tones, yellow, and wood, then writing a helper function that mixes a base and highlight color using smoothstep against the surface normal plus some noise for variation, confirming that `mix`, `noise`, `smoothstep`, and `paint` are all exported from the SDK. Now I'm applying a scale pattern across the dragon's neck and head using red and deep gold.

I'm planning the mane as extruded flame-like blades, then drafting the actual import statement pulling in the geometry builder, random/curve utilities, paint helpers, and pattern functions like scales, stripes, countershade, mottle, gradient, and svg, while weighing whether to import glow from a separate kit path or implement the glow effect manually to avoid import risk.

Deciding to use the glow kit since it clones materials rather than mutating shared ones, then sizing the paint atlas to roughly 2048px based on painted surface area and desired texel density. Now I'm sketching coordinate helper functions defining the hull's stern and bow z-positions and a rise function for the hull profile along its length.

Still refining the hull geometry...

I need to figure out how to sample the path to get z-to-t mapping, since the API for querying a point along the path by parameter is ambiguous about whether it returns a Vector3 directly or a point object with coordinate properties.

Confirming it returns a Vector3 since the docs show vector subtraction on the result, so I'll define a helper that maps a parameter to its z-coordinate along the path. Then I'm planning the hull pieces, starting with a floor slab swept along the centerline using a box cross-section, where the sweep's normal direction needs to align with "up" since the path lies in the YZ plane.

The floor's bottom sits exactly at zero when there's no rise, which checks out, and since there are no joints in the path there's no need for smoothing. For the walls, I'm sweeping along a path offset in x by the half-width minus a margin, using a box section with varying radius, but worrying that strong variation in half-width near the ends will tilt the wall's orientation since the box's axes follow the path's tangent and binormal.

Now I'm defining a paint function for the walls that checks surface normal and height to assign colors — gold for the top near the rail, a deep red lacquer mix for interior faces, black for a band below the gold trim, and teal near the bottom.

Then I'm positioning the rail along the hull edge, offsetting it slightly outward from the wall's outer face, sizing its cross-section, and preparing to paint black and gold stripes on it.

Now I'm figuring out how to close off the gap left at the bow where the walls end, planning to fill it with a stem post shape swept along the center path.

The dragon neck and tail bases at prow and stern naturally hide the block tops, so I don't need a separate cap there. For the deck floors, I'm planning dark lacquered plank-style paint using striped color bands along the z-axis, applied wherever the surface normal points up and the point sits above the floor level.

For benches, I'm sizing each seat box to span between the hull walls at that row, positioned at a seat height above the floor, painted in deep red lacquer with gold accents at the ends.

Now I'm designing the paddler figure: hips as a dark shorts box sitting on the seat, with a tapered torso frustum leaning from the pelvis upward and forward to suggest paddling posture.

Then I'm placing the shoulders symmetrically outward from the torso center, and adding a head sphere slightly forward of the shoulders, letting it overlap the torso top so I can skip a separate neck piece.

Actually, let me add a thin neck rod connecting torso to head for better proportions. Then I'm working out the paddle geometry, positioning the grip point near the shoulder offset and extending the blade tip outward, checking that it clears neighboring seats at that row spacing.

Now I'm computing hand positions along the paddle shaft direction, placing the upper and lower grip hands and checking their distance from inner and outer shoulders stays within reasonable arm reach, then finding elbow midpoints with an outward bend for the inner arm.

For the outer arm I'm doing the same elbow-offset calculation between shoulder and lower hand, verifying arm segment lengths add up correctly, then thinking about how to texture the sleeves using banded sweeps that transition from shirt color to skin color partway down the arm.

Now I'm working out the seated leg geometry: hip, knee, and ankle positions with forward-bent thighs, factoring in seat height and floor level to get the proportions right.

I'm adding a dark foot box and calf segment connecting knee to ankle, then checking row spacing so feet don't collide with the bench or pelvis of the paddler in the row ahead.

Setting shorts versus skin coloring along the leg sweep based on position. Checking if the last row's extended legs collide with the drum position near z=3.5, and shifting the row z-coordinates slightly to avoid the overlap.

I'm working out eight paddler rows times two paddlers each for sixteen total, alternating shirt colors by row and varying skin tones by index parity, with red headbands throughout and the steerer positioned behind the final row.

Now I'm defining the dragon head geometry, setting up a base center point and sketching the neck curve as a spline running from the hull up toward the prow.

Building the collar ring...

Now I'm laying out the head geometry in detail—placing the skull sphere, snout frustum, nose bulb, and nostril spheres with specific positions and radii to build a recognizable facial structure facing forward.

Still shaping the jaw geometry...

Placing gold-irised eye spheres with a decal for the pupil and outline, oriented to face outward, then adding a heavy brow ridge above each eye.

Now sweeping a tapered bezier curve from the inner brow outward and back to form a hooded ridge in deep red-gold, then starting to shape horn bases at the back of the skull that will sweep upward into tips.

Skipping ear fins, moving to the mane instead — placing flame-shaped blades along the back of the neck, computing positions by offsetting points along the neck path backward and upward, oriented to flare up-and-back from the skull toward the body.

Still working out flame outline coordinates...

I'll skip corner-smoothing to avoid edge-crossing risk, keeping the shape faceted since it's low-poly anyway. For the paint, I'm defining a color mix from red to gold based on height along the extruded outline, scaled by the flame's size factor.

Now I'm planning the mane layout: six flames sweeping from the neck up to the back of the head, plus cheek flames extruded sideways and a beard with five bezier strands from the chin tip.

Adding whiskers next...

Adding cheek puffs near the jaw hinge for dimension, then thinking about whether to skip a decorative neck-collar/bell detail. For the tail, I'm sketching a sweeping curve that curls up from the stern, over the deck, arcing forward above the steerer's head.

I'm adjusting the tail's endpoint to give the steerer clearance, repositioning them slightly to avoid collision with the tail tip. I'm tapering the tail's radius and planning flame-shaped fins along its outer curve, plus a fan of three larger flames at the tip, computing the outward offset direction from the curve's tangent to place them correctly.

Rotating the tangent 90° around X to get the outward normal, but I'm second-guessing which side actually faces outward since the tail curve bends from heading backward to heading upward — the center of curvature shifts depending on segment, so I need to work out orientation per-segment rather than assuming a fixed sign for the fins along the dragon's back ridge.

I should just compute it generically: estimate the center of curvature from the change in tangent between two nearby points, then take the outward direction as the negation of that vector. I'm defining an `outward(path, t)` helper that samples tangents slightly before and after t to get this direction, so it works for any curve shape without me reasoning through each segment manually — I can reuse it for the neck mane too, maybe blending with a manual direction there since the neck's curvature flips in a way that's less intuitive.

For the neck mane I'll keep it simple: use a fixed backward-leaning direction and offset points slightly up and back from the neck's centerline to place the blade bases. For the tail fins, I'll use the tangent as one axis and the outward vector as the other, positioning points along the outward direction scaled by the radius — I don't think these two axes strictly need to be perpendicular since it's just for extrusion thickness.

For the tail tip, I want three fanned flames with slightly different orientations, roughly using the tangent plus varying outward-biased directions to create a spread effect at the tail's endpoint near the back of the creature.

Setting up a flame helper function that extrudes shapes using tip position, direction vectors, scale, and color...

Now I'm working out the steerer's position, calculating floor height at that point along the curved hull profile to figure out where to place their feet, hips, torso, and head.

Checking hull width at the stern to make sure the steerer's stance fits inboard, then routing the steering oar to the side so it avoids colliding with the tail-curl structure at the stern, running from the steerer's hands outward and down.

Checking the oar stays clear of the hull at various z-points confirms it's outside the boat's width. I'll skip the fulcrum post detail and move to positioning the steerer's arms, placing shoulders and grip points so the hands align naturally along the oar.

Testing a few coordinate sets for the grip and lower hand point shows the arm length coming out too long relative to the shoulder position, so I'm adjusting the oar's z-location and shoulder placement closer together until the arm distance falls within a plausible reach.

I'm also working out the floor height formula along the hull's curve to position standing legs correctly, and sketching the steerer figure wearing a black-and-gold jacket with a conical straw hat.

Now I'm turning to the drummer, seated on a stool facing backward, and planning a general person-building function that takes position, seat height, facing direction, and clothing/skin details as parameters so I can reuse it across characters.

I'm working out the stool height and body proportions at the drummer's position along the curved deck, calculating floor elevation from the rise formula, then stacking stool top, hip center, torso, and head heights to place the drummer accurately.

For clothing, I'll give the drummer a black shirt with gold collar stripes and a red sash waist, plus a gold headband with pompom, facing away from the boat's +Z direction. I'm now positioning his shoulders, hands, and drumsticks relative to the drum center to figure out the stick geometry for mid-strike poses.

Working out stick angles so the tip hits the drumhead surface near z=3.82-3.85 while keeping the back end of the stick clear of the torso, adjusting hand position to around z=4.0-4.05 accordingly.

For the raised stick I'm placing the hand, tip, and back end coordinates, and setting shoulder and elbow positions with elbows angled outward.

Checking drum height against hand position to confirm the striking point sits correctly on the drumhead surface.

Now I'm working out the drum stand geometry, trying an A-frame with crossed legs and verifying the foot positions stay within the floor hull and clear of the drum radius.

Poles outside the drum area won't work, so I'm repositioning them onto the rail near the stern, computing the hull width and rise there to anchor the pole base, extending each pole upward about 1.75 units. Now I'm shaping a swallowtail pennant outline to extrude backward off the pole.

Now I'm defining the swallowtail pennant polygon with a notched trailing edge, mounting it just below the pole top, and planning a thin textured emblem plane on each face near the hoist to show a decorative insignia.

I'll reuse the drum's swirl texture for the pennant emblems to save on resources, then move on to designing the lantern atop the pole: a glowing red sphere scaled to a lantern shape with gold cylinder caps and a tassel, sitting directly on top with a finial rather than hanging from an arm.

I'm checking that everything stays above the ground plane, with the hull bottom at zero and antler tips, flags, and lantern reaching up to around 2.6 units, which all looks proportionate.

Now I'm writing the SVG texture strings, starting with a gold cloud pattern made of smooth curved stroke paths...

Writing cloud SVG code...

Still writing eye details...

Finishing the eye path, then clipping an iris circle inside the almond shape using a matching clipPath. For the left eye I just mirror the right eye's drawing per the toon kit convention. Then I'm setting up the drum swirl texture on a circle geometry with a cream background and a red ring for cropping.

Drawing a festive red-and-gold yin-yang emblem: a dark red outer circle, a cream inner circle with gold stroke, a swirling two-tone path split into red and cream halves, plus small accent dots and an outline ring.

Now adding a ring of twelve gold dots around the red rim, then sketching the forehead pearl -- a red circle with gold outline surrounded by a flame-shaped gold motif. I'm skipping the tuft and beard details for now and considering a small decorative plaque or number-sign element for texture.

Instead of painting waves, I'm swapping in a repeating wave-crest decal near the waterline -- cream curling shapes with teal outlines, tiled across the hull using a translated loop.

I'm figuring out decal placement and counts: around 5 wave decals and 5 cloud decals per side (20 total parts), each a low-poly grid mesh, placed against the wall's outer sweep surface at the correct height and width to wrap around the hull curvature.

Still sizing cloud decals...

Setting wave and cloud positions within the teal band, then roughing out a part count estimate across the whole dragon boat: hull, rails, benches, paddlers and paddles, dragon head/tail, drum, steering, flags, and decals, tallying toward a total piece count.

I'm also reviewing the API details I'll need — part geometry calls, frustum/capsule/rod helpers, color/paint reuse across parts, flat-shading options, and extrude parameters — to make sure the build script stays consistent.

For flame rendering, I'm planning to cache paint objects by size to avoid creating excessive unique materials, defining a few standard flame sizes (small, medium, large) with a shared thickness constant. Starting the TypeScript setup now...

Writing imports and setup...

Defining the lacquer color presets for red, gold, black, and jade materials, then setting up the builder function with hull cross-section positions along the z-axis.

Now I'm writing a track helper that builds a spline path from these z positions plus a rise and optional lateral offset function, along with a helper to sample the z-coordinate at any point along that path. I'm weighing how to type the path parameter without fighting the catmull return type, likely settling on a loose structural type with an `at` method.

Then I'm constructing the floor as a swept box section along a flattened version of the track, with a half-width function driving the sweep radius at each point, and thinking through the default orientation frame (since no explicit up vector is given) to make sure the normal and binormal align sensibly for a path running from stern to bow.

Still writing sweep code...

Adding block top faces with black lacquer paint, then defining rail geometry with striped black-and-gold paint for the side tracks.

Now I'm checking that rails meet cleanly near the end walls, then placing a row of bench boxes along the z-axis, each sized to fit within the wall width at that position.

I'm skipping gold end caps on the bench to avoid protrusion, and confirming bench placement works without explicit joints since static geometry stays under root. I'm checking the bench sits embedded slightly in the wall thickness, but notice there might be a visible gap between the bench and floor that needs support legs.

Now I'm positioning two support blocks under the bench, calculating their height so they span from the floor top to the bench bottom, and placing them inboard enough that they don't collide with the figures' legs resting against the bench.

One center support per bench is enough, since outer walls handle lateral support. I'm now defining the paddler function that positions each figure at offset sx, applying shirt and skin tones with stripe tinting.

For the shirt coloring, I'm setting up horizontal banded patterns (jersey hoops) using the stripes function with y-axis bands, and considering a custom paint function that adds a colored collar band near the top of the torso.

I'm defining a reusable shirtPaint helper that colors the collar differently from the base shirt — red collar for yellow shirts, cream for jade — applied only to the torso region above a certain y-threshold, while sleeves keep a flat base color. For the head, I'm adding a small sphere for skin detail, and positioning everything using arrays of coordinates.

I set up a vector helper and a tuple-based position helper, then start building the paddler figure: hips as a box in shorts color, and a tilted frustum shape for the torso/shirt that angles forward slightly along its axis.

Now I'm sketching the shoulders, neck rod, and head components — a sphere for the head, hair, headband, and eyes — while deciding to skip finer details like ears, nose, and mouth to keep things simple.

I'm finding the headband keeps clipping through the hair at the back, and when I recenter it to fix that, the head geometry instead pokes through the band at the front — so I need to adjust the band's position and radius to clear both surfaces.

I'm reworking the headband shape to be elliptical rather than circular, scaling it along z so it sits closer to the forehead without ballooning out, and accepting minor overlap with the hair as a stylized simplification. I'll treat the hair as a cap sitting above the band line rather than fully enclosing it.

I'm settling on reasonable constants without being able to visually verify, so I'll simplify the paddler's head to a skin sphere, hair cap, headband cylinder, eyes, and a small red knot box at the back. Now I'm moving on to building out the arm positions and geometry.

Working out shoulder, hand, and elbow coordinates for inner and outer arms, then sweeping polylines through them with rounded corners to form the sleeves...

Writing paddle shaft and blade geometry...

Setting up the paddle blade paint logic with gold tip and red lacquer coloring, then starting the leg geometry sweep...

Checking foot box height placement, then spacing feet and paddlers along z with small random jitter for natural variation. Now I'm starting the dragon head/neck geometry, defining the neck as a smooth curve of points rising and extending forward from the body.

I'm checking that the neck's radius doesn't exceed the hull's width at the bow so it doesn't stick out oddly -- the neck base radius of 0.2 is too wide compared to the hull half-width there, so I'm narrowing it to around 0.15 to keep it flush with the bow block.

Placing the skull with radii and checking it meets the neck cleanly, then setting up mane flames along the back of the neck and skull rear using positioned t-values and directional offsets, planning a mirrorBoth helper for symmetric head details.

Now I'm working out the eye geometry—small bulging spheres placed just outside the skull ellipsoid surface at mirrored x-coordinates, with decals applied along the outward normal direction, checking the math confirms the eyes protrude slightly as intended.

Then I'm adding brow sweeps above the eyes and upper jaw detailing, like curling lip flares running from the cheeks toward the snout tip for a moustache-like effect.

Now I'm defining the antler geometry with curved bezier paths branching upward and outward from a base point near the forehead...

Still writing tine geometry...
